title: Computer Science
body:
A map of the degree, a B.Sc. in Computer Science with a concentration in Mathematics. Every
course below has its own index note, written to be read start to finish, and everything else
in the vault hangs off one of them.

The COMP courses build a machine from the bottom up and then ask what it can do. First year
writes programs in two languages, one that hides the machine and one that shows it. Second
year opens the machine, covering the processor, the logic gates inside it, the structures a
program keeps its data in, and the theory of what a machine can compute at all. Third year
adds the layers built on top: an operating system, a web stack, and a language with no
mutable state. Fourth year returns to the questions second year raised and answers them
properly.

The MATH courses supply what the fourth-year material runs on. Calculus produces the
derivative, which is what every optimiser follows downhill. Linear algebra produces the matrix
product, which is what a neural network computes. Statistics produces the vocabulary for
saying how much to trust a result. Abstract algebra produces the finite fields that
cryptography is built from.

The two tracks meet in fourth year, where [[MACHINE LEARNING]] is calculus and linear algebra
under a new vocabulary, and [[MATH 4TH YEAR/MATH 4111/CRYPTOGRAPHY|CRYPTOGRAPHY]] is a term of
applying [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]].

---

## First year

- **[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE]]**: the first programming course, in Python, on
  turning a problem statement into steps a machine can execute. Assumes no experience, and
  defines every term it uses.
- **[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]]**: the same job in C++, where every type is
  declared and memory is managed by hand. Pointers, the stack and the heap.
- **[[CALCULUS 1]]**: limits, and the two constructions they produce, the derivative and the
  integral.
- **[[LINEAR ALGEBRA]]**: linear systems, and the vectors, matrices and transformations that
  solve them.
- **[[STATISTICS]]**: reasoning from a sample to the population, and quantifying how far off
  that reasoning might be.
- **[[SYMBOLIC LOGIC]]**: deciding whether an argument works by translating it into a formal
  system and applying a rule.
- **[[CLASSICAL PHYSICS 1]]**: Newtonian mechanics, from describing motion to the conservation
  laws that answer without tracking it.
- **[[THE UNIVERSE AT LARGE]]**: (Elective) what can be worked out about stars and galaxies from the
  light that reaches a telescope.

## Second year

- **[[COMPUTING MACHINERY]]**: what the machine does with a program, written in MC68000
  assembly with no compiler in between.
- **[[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]]**: down into the gates and out to the devices, covering logic
  circuits, polling, interrupts and DMA.
- **[[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]]**: six containers in Java, and the habit of pricing an
  operation before choosing the structure that performs it.
- **[[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]]**: the work surrounding the code, from finding
  out what to build to keeping it changeable afterwards.
- **[[DISCRETE MATH]]**: the mathematics of countable objects, and where proving a claim
  replaces testing it.
- **[[CALCULUS 2]]**: integration in full, then infinite series.
- **[[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]]**: linear algebra pointed at datasets, where the
  system has no solution and the answer is a projection.

## Third year

- **[[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]**: calculus once the input is a point and the output is a vector,
  covering multivariable calculus and differential equations.
- **[[OPERATING SYSTEMS]]**: the layer between programs and hardware, organised around
  synchronization.
- **[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]]**: which problems can be computed at all, and how much
  machine each one requires.
- **[[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]]**: the whole stack in order, from DNS and HTTP up to the DOM
  and the code that manipulates it.
- **[[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]]**: groups, rings and fields, where the rules are named first and
  everything else is proved from them.
- **[[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]]**: functional programming in Haskell, with lambda calculus as
  the formal model.
- **[[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]]**: designing an algorithm, proving a bound on it, and
  handling the problems where no efficient algorithm exists.
- **[[HUMAN COMPUTER INTERACTION]]**: measuring software against a person instead of against
  the machine, and treating usability as something designed and tested.
- **[[INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY AND SOCIETY]]**: what happens after software ships, and the
  ethical frameworks for arguing about whether it should have been built.

## Fourth year

- **[[MATH 4TH YEAR/MATH 4111/CRYPTOGRAPHY|CRYPTOGRAPHY]]**: where abstract algebra becomes
  deployed software, in RSA, Diffie-Hellman and elliptic curves.
- **[[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]]**: any function as a sum of simple waves, which converts
  hard operations into easy ones.
- **[[ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE]]**: building systems that decide, organised around the rational
  agent.
- **[[MACHINE LEARNING]]**: fitting parameters when the algorithm cannot be written down.
  Choose a model family, define a loss, and let optimisation select the rest.
- **[[DIRECTED READING]]**: a four-person senior project on statistics in finance, producing a
  risk dashboard and a research report on how sentiment moves markets.

---

## Beyond coursework

- **[[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]]**: Dewdney's 66 self-contained chapters, filed by the course
  each one sits beside.
- **[[Web Interview Prep]]**: web fundamentals rebuilt around one question, which machine does
  this actually run on.
- **[[Leetcode]]**: a routing guide from the shape of the input to the pattern that solves it.

## How the notes are written

Every index above follows one format, specified in `_meta/index-style.md`: an opening saying
what the course covers and what it assumes, topic sections in teaching order so nothing is
used before it is defined, a worked example wherever one helps, and a closing list of the
courses on either side of it. The aim is that a reader can learn the subject from the index
and reach for the child notes for depth.
